topic: Philosophical reflections on mathematical work: criticism versus systematising, Klein's applied versus Hilbert's ideal aims, why problems from physics seem richer and more intuitive (with an example from memory feats), layers of axioms, and the axiomatic method as the method of the future.

triage.modern_statement: This isn't a mathematical research question. Hilbert is asking a philosophical, epistemological question: what does it mean to call a mathematical problem or concept 'anschaulich' (intuitive or visualizable)? The context is his remark that problems from physics seem richer and more intuitive than others. It belongs to the long debate about how Anschauung (intuition, in the Kantian sense of perception and imagination) relates to the formal axiomatic method. No theorem or conjecture can be stated in modern terms.
triage.answered_by: There is no mathematical answer. Hilbert came back to the role of intuition several times: in his axiomatic work on geometry and physics, in his finitist proof theory of the 1920s (which builds on 'concrete, intuitive' finite objects), and in the book 'Anschauliche Geometrie' (1932, written with S. Cohn-Vossen). Historians such as L. Corry and M. Hallett have studied his view of Anschauung. Most of these links come from general knowledge of Hilbert's work; the searches directly confirmed only the 1932 book and the existence of the historical studies.

evidence.claim: Historians have analysed Hilbert's unpublished lecture notes (1891–1905) on how geometry, formalism and intuition relate under the axiomatic method.

There is a scholarly study of intuition and the axiomatic method in Hilbert's foundations of physics, including Kantian background. This matches the page's comparison of physics-based problems with intuitiveness.
In 1932 Hilbert and Cohn-Vossen published 'Anschauliche Geometrie', which presents geometry in an intuitive, visual way.
Philosophers discuss whether Hilbert's axiomatic programme was meant to give a complete analysis of mathematical intuition.

triage.why: The note is a rhetorical, conceptual question inside philosophical reflections on mathematical method. It isn't among the 23 problems or the 24th problem, and it doesn't pose a well-defined mathematical problem. The nature of mathematical intuition is still discussed in philosophy and history of mathematics, but that is not a mathematical research area, so 'active_today' is marked unclear.
